13 In a large container in an oil refinery, three oils of different densities are mixed. No chemical
activity occurs.
The mixture consists of
1200 kg of oil of density 1100 kg m–3,
1500 kg of oil of density 860 kg m–3,
4000 kg of oil of density 910 kg m–3.
What is the density of the mixture?
A
927 kg m–3
B
957 kg m–3
C
1010 kg m–3
D
1080 kg m–3

hints: Notice you are given three masses $1200 \text{ kg}$, $1500 \text{ kg}$ and $4000 \text{ kg}$, not volumes, so you cannot average the three densities directly.
Recall $\rho = m/V$, so each separate oil occupies volume $V = m/\rho$ using its own $1100$, $860$ and $910 \text{ kg m}^{-3}$ values.
Add the three masses for total mass and add the three $m/\rho$ volumes for total volume, then use $\rho_{mix} = \text{total mass}/\text{total volume}$.
walkthrough: Total mass is the sum of the masses: $m = 1200 + 1500 + 4000 = 6700 \text{ kg}$.
Density is defined by $\rho = m/V$, so volume is $V = m/\rho$. With no chemical activity the mixture volume is the sum of the three oil volumes.
Mixture density $\rho_{mix} = 6700/7.231 \approx 927 \text{ kg m}^{-3}$ with unit check $\text{kg}/\text{m}^3$. This is option A.

A.explanation: Total mass $6700 \text{ kg}$ divided by total volume about $7.23 \text{ m}^3$ gives about $927 \text{ kg m}^{-3}$.

B.explanation: This is close to the mass-weighted mean of the densities, which is wrong because equal masses do not contribute equal volumes.

C.explanation: This value is too high because it treats density as additive by mass rather than calculating $V = m/\rho$ for each oil.

D.explanation: This value is near the highest density $1100 \text{ kg m}^{-3}$ and ignores the large volumes of the two lower-density oils.
